en: The Sūtra on the Twelve Categories of Birth and Death, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Khotan during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Monastery. At that time...
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall preach a sutra for you.
The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will graciously accept our instructions.
The Buddha said:
“There are twelve categories of those who die. What are these twelve?
First is the one who dies without remainder, namely the Arhat who is free from attachments;
second is the one who has transcended death, namely the Anāgāmin who does not return.”
The third is death with remainder, which refers to the *sakṛdāgāmin* who goes and returns;
the fourth is death through training, which refers to the *srotāpanna* who has seen the path;
the fifth is death without deception, which refers to those of the eight classes of noble ones.
Sixth is "dying with joy," which refers to one who practices single-mindedness;
seventh is "repeated death," which refers to a person of immoral conduct;
eighth is "death with regret," which refers to an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
The ninth is death by misfortune, which refers to the suffering of the solitary and destitute;
the tenth is death through bondage and attachment, which refers to the animal realm;
the eleventh is death by burning and rotting, which refers to the hells.
The twelfth is those who die of hunger and thirst; these are the hungry ghosts (*preta*). "Bhikṣus!

You should understand this clearly and train yourselves accordingly: do not be negligent, do not give rise to lustful desire for forms, stay far away from all calamities, and with a pure mind, constantly bring to fulfillment that which has not yet been realized."
Why is this? To die repeatedly is extreme suffering;

to die with regret is also suffering; to die by untimely means is most violent; to die while bound by attachments is likewise violent; to die burned and mangled is most painful; and to die of hunger and thirst is also painful.
Thus, bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way:
practice dwelling in seclusion, whether under a tree or elsewhere, training in single-minded dhyāna; do not be frivolous or playful, lest you later regret it.
"This is the Buddha’s teaching; this is the Dharma of the Buddha.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus rejoiced, bowed their heads in prostration, and withdrew.
*The Sūtra on the Twelve Categories of Birth and Death*.
